units.title: Queries, keys, values and scaled dot-product attention
outcomes: Derive the \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) scale from unit-variance query and key components and state the assumption it needs.
Implement stable scaled dot-product attention from tensor operations, with a row-wise softmax that cannot overflow in `fp32`.
Explain attention output as a convex combination of values and predict how a logit shift moves the weights.
units.why: Attention is the only communication path between positions in a transformer. If the scale, the softmax axis or the stability fix is wrong, every later block inherits the error.

study.title: Equivalent-implementation box
study.locator: The Efficient implementation equivalent code box: default scale \(1/\sqrt{E}\), score-times-scale order, and softmax-then-dropout order

focus: Queries, keys and values are three learned linear maps of the same input. D2L builds them bias-free by default while UDL equations 12.4 and 12.6 carry bias vectors, so the two parameter counts differ by construction.

Under independent zero-mean unit-variance components, \(q^\top k\) has variance \(d\). The \(1/\sqrt{d}\) factor restores unit variance before the softmax; without it large \(d\) saturates the softmax and gradients vanish.

Stable softmax subtracts the row max first. Naive `fp32` softmax on the UDL Problem 12.4 logits overflows at \(\exp(100)\): that entry becomes `inf/inf`, which is `NaN`, and the rest become `0`. The shifted form returns the correct weights.

UDL lays inputs out as \(D \times N\) columns with softmax per column; D2L uses batch by queries by keys with softmax on the last axis. In both, exactly one axis sums to 1: check which one before reading any heatmap.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive the \(1/\sqrt{d}\) scale from the variance argument. Then hand-compute the Deep-ML 490 first test: scores \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}0.7071&0\\0&0.7071\end{smallmatrix}\right]\), weights \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}0.6698&0.3302\\0.3302&0.6698\end{smallmatrix}\right]\), output \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1.6605&2.6605\\2.3395&3.3395\end{smallmatrix}\right]\).
traps: Computing softmax as \(\exp(z)/\sum(\exp(z))\) in `fp32`. \(\exp(100)\) overflows to `inf`, so the sum is `inf`, the large entry becomes `NaN` and every other entry `0`. Always subtract the row max, and recheck any code that skips it.
Softmaxing the wrong axis after a transpose. UDL and D2L sum over different axes by layout; a heatmap that sums to 1 along queries instead of keys inverts the routing story.
Quoting D2L parameter counts for UDL equations or vice versa. The bias terms add \(3D\) parameters; carry them only when the equations you implement include them.

selfTest.q: Query and key components are independent with zero mean and unit variance, in dimension \(d\). What are the mean and variance of their dot product, and what scale restores unit variance?
selfTest.a: Mean 0 and variance \(d\), since the dot product sums \(d\) independent unit-variance products. Multiply by \(1/\sqrt{d}\) to restore unit variance before the softmax.

selfTest.q: Naive `fp32` softmax meets UDL Problem 12.4 logits `[-3, 1, 100, 5, -1]`. What comes out, what does the max-subtracted form give, and what do the 25 derivatives say?
selfTest.a: Naive \(\exp\) overflows at \(\exp(100)\), so the denominator is `inf` and the output is `[0, 0, NaN, 0, 0]`. Max-subtracted softmax gives \(y_3\) near 1 and the rest near 0. All 25 derivatives are near 0 (largest magnitude about 5.5e-42): a saturated softmax with vanishing gradients.

selfTest.q: A self-attention block takes \(N = 5\) inputs of width \(D = 8\), with queries, keys and values also width 8. How many QKV weights and biases, how many attention weights, and how many weights and biases in a fully connected \(DN\) to \(DN\) map?
selfTest.a: QKV: 3 times (64 + 8) = 216. Attention weights: 25. Fully connected: 1600 weights plus 40 biases = 1640.

selfTest.q: Why must attention weights be nonnegative and sum to one, and where does each output lie?
selfTest.a: They form a convex combination, so each output is a weighted average of the value vectors and lies in their convex hull. Routing language only makes sense under this constraint.

study.title: Mask semantics, causality and dropout
study.locator: The boolean-mask Note (`True` means participate, inverse of `MultiheadAttention` `key_padding_mask`), the `is_causal` parameter entry including the non-square upper-left bias, and the dropout Warning that dropout applies in every mode

focus: Padding and causal masks compose by intersection: a score survives only if both allow it. D2L `valid_lens` expresses padding lengths, the decoder \([1..n]\) rows express causality, and a real batch needs both at once.
Mask value conventions differ by API. SDPA bool `True` means participate while `MultiheadAttention` `key_padding_mask` `True` means mask out. Copying one convention into the other leaks padding.

A fully masked row has no agreed meaning. D2L `-1e6` gives uniform weights, all `-inf` through plain softmax gives `NaN`, and SDPA on CPU returned zeros in version 2.14. Test your convention instead of assuming one.
SDPA applies `dropout_p` in every mode. Pass `0.0` outside training or evaluation outputs stay stochastic.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, build combined causal plus padding masks for two sequences of valid lengths 3 and 2 over 4 keys, show every disallowed weight is exactly `0`, then change a future token and a padded value and show the earlier valid outputs do not move.
traps: Trusting uniform weights on a fully masked row. D2L returns \(1/n\) there, so padding values still mix into the output unless you zero the row downstream.
Passing both `attn_mask` and `is_causal` to SDPA. The function raises an error; pick one expression of the same mask.
Leaving `dropout_p` nonzero during evaluation or testing. Outputs differ run to run and differential tests against a manual path fail for no structural reason.

selfTest.q: D2L `masked_softmax` meets a row with valid length 0 over 4 keys. What weights come out and why is that dangerous?
selfTest.a: Uniform weights `0.25` each: all four `-1e6` entries softmax equally. The output mixes padding values with full weight, so the row must be zeroed or excluded downstream.

selfTest.q: An SDPA bool mask marks padding as `True`. What happens, and how does `MultiheadAttention` `key_padding_mask` differ?
selfTest.a: SDPA treats `True` as participate, so padding joins attention: a leak. `MultiheadAttention` `key_padding_mask` uses the inverse convention, `True` means mask out. Invert when migrating.

selfTest.q: Why is a future-token intervention a stronger causal proof than reading attention weights?
selfTest.a: Weights show one layer; dropout, residuals and later layers remix paths. Perturbing a future token and requiring earlier outputs to stay fixed tests the composed block, including leaks through paths the weight plot never shows.

selfTest.q: SDPA is called with `dropout_p` `0.5` during evaluation. What goes wrong?
selfTest.a: Dropout still applies in every mode, so outputs stay stochastic. Pass `0.0` when the caller is not training.

study.title: Decoder self versus encoder-decoder attention
study.locator: `TransformerDecoderBlock`: `attention1` over `(X, key_values, key_values)` with `dec_valid_lens` versus `attention2` over `(Y, enc_outputs, enc_outputs)` with `enc_valid_lens`

focus: D2L sets per-head width to `num_hiddens` over `num_heads`, so all four projections stay `num_hiddens` by `num_hiddens`. The head count changes mixing, not size.

Heads fold into the batch axis: `(batch, steps, heads, width)` becomes `(batch times heads, steps, width)` for the shared attention call, then unfolds back. `valid_lens` must repeat once per head to stay aligned.
Cross-attention reuses the identical math with different sources: queries from the decoder state, keys and values from encoder outputs, with padding-only lengths.
UDL Problem 12.5 is the cost intuition: narrow heads at fixed total width keep the implementation efficient.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, walk shapes for batch 2, 4 queries, width 100, 5 heads: projections stay `(2, 4, 100)`, folded per-head tensors are `(10, 4, 20)`, concatenation restores `(2, 4, 100)`. State BERT per-head width 64 from 1024 over 16 heads.
traps: Folding heads with one `reshape`. Going straight from `(batch, steps, hidden)` to `(batch times heads, steps, hidden/heads)` runs without error but gives each head a mix of positions. Split hidden into `(heads, head width)`, move the head axis next to batch, then merge, as `transpose_qkv` does.

Repeating `valid_lens` in the wrong order. D2L folds batch-major, so lengths need `repeat_interleave` (`[l0, l0, l1, l1]`). Tiling with `repeat` (`[l0, l1, l0, l1]`) has the right length and silently masks heads with another example's length. Dropping the `repeat` fails loudly in `masked_softmax`.
Assuming cross-attention needs a new formula. Only the sources change; calling self-attention with (Y, encoder outputs, encoder outputs) is the whole difference.

selfTest.q: BERT uses width 1024 with 16 heads. What is the per-head width, and what shape are its per-head query matrices?
selfTest.a: 64. Each per-head query, key and value matrix is \(64 \times 1024\).

selfTest.q: Why does fixing total width while varying head count hold parameters and compute flat?
selfTest.a: All four projections stay `num_hiddens` by `num_hiddens` regardless of head count, so QKVO parameters stay 4 times width squared and per-head matmuls sum back to the same total.

selfTest.q: In the D2L decoder block, which tensors supply queries, keys and values to the second attention call, and which lengths mask it?
selfTest.a: Queries come from the decoder state `Y` after self-attention; keys and values come from encoder outputs. Only encoder padding lengths mask it; there is no causal mask on this call.

selfTest.q: The `valid_lens` `repeat` per head is deleted. What breaks?
selfTest.a: The folded batch has batch times heads rows but only batch lengths, so D2L `masked_softmax` fails with a mask shape error. The silent form of the bug is tiling with `repeat` instead of `repeat_interleave`: the count matches, but heads use another example's length.

study.title: Order-free self-attention
study.locator: The paragraphs before Positional Encoding on parallel computation discarding sequential order

focus: Without positions the block is permutation-equivariant: \(\operatorname{Sa}[XP]\) equals \(\operatorname{Sa}[X]P\). UDL Problem 12.3 asks for this proof; it is the reason order must be injected as input.
Absolute encodings add a unique column per position. The D2L `TransformerEncoder` scales embeddings by \(\sqrt{\text{width}}\) before the add because the encodings stay in \([-1, 1]\).

Sinusoid pairs rotate with offset: position \(i\) plus \(\delta\) is a fixed \(2 \times 2\) rotation of position \(i\), depending on \(\delta\) and frequency only. Shifting text shifts encodings linearly.
Relative schemes index by the offset between key and query positions, not by absolute index. They survive absolute shifts that absolute tables must relearn.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write \(p(i, 2j)\) and \(p(i, 2j+1)\), sketch the \(\operatorname{Sa}[XP]\) equals \(\operatorname{Sa}[X]P\) proof, and verify the \(2 \times 2\) rotation numerically for one \((i, \delta, j)\) triple.
traps: Not stating where positions enter. UDL lists three placements: once at the input, at every layer, or only in the query and key computation. The last leaves values free of position, which changes what later layers can read; write down which one your block uses.
Exceeding D2L `max_len` 1000. The stored table is fixed width, so longer inputs fail on the add; rebuild the table instead of truncating silently.

Comparing encodings or outputs in train mode. D2L applies dropout to the sum of embeddings and encodings, so train-mode runs drop entries at random; compare in eval mode or with dropout `0`, as the D2L plot does.

selfTest.q: State permutation equivariance for self-attention and explain why it forces positional input.
selfTest.a: \(\operatorname{Sa}[XP]\) equals \(\operatorname{Sa}[X]P\) for any permutation matrix \(P\): reordering inputs reorders outputs identically. The block therefore carries no order information, so positions must enter as extra input.

selfTest.q: Write the D2L sinusoidal encoding entries.
selfTest.a: \(p(i, 2j)\) equals \(\sin(i / 10000^{2j/d})\) and \(p(i, 2j+1)\) equals \(\cos(i / 10000^{2j/d})\), with \(i\) the position and \(d\) the width.

selfTest.q: What does the \(2 \times 2\) rotation from position \(i\) to position \(i\) plus \(\delta\) depend on?
selfTest.a: Only the offset \(\delta\) and the pair frequency \(\omega_j\). It never depends on the absolute position \(i\), which is why a fixed shift is a fixed linear map.

selfTest.q: A 1500-token input meets D2L default `PositionalEncoding`. What happens?
selfTest.a: The stored table is 1000 wide, so the slice caps at 1000 and the add fails on shape mismatch. Rebuild the encoding with a larger `max_len`.

study.title: Pre-norm vision transformer block
study.locator: `ViTBlock` with its pre-versus-post-normalization paragraph, `PatchEmbedding` with the `(96, 16, 512)` shape check, and Putting It All Together for encoder-only assembly
study.depth: Skip Training; the Fashion-MNIST run is not part of this unit.

focus: Post-norm (UDL equation 12.13, D2L encoder) normalizes after each residual add; pre-norm (`ViTBlock`) normalizes the branch inputs and adds untouched residuals. D2L states pre-norm trains more effectively.
Residuals force equal widths: D2L requires decoder `num_hiddens` to equal the encoder width for the adds and the cross \(QK^\top\) product.

Neither D2L MLP is gated: `PositionWiseFFN` is `ReLU` and `ViTMLP` is `GELU` with dropout. A gated block adds a third projection and an elementwise product; hold parameters fixed by shrinking width, not by ignoring the extra matrix.

Pattern follows context: BERT-style encoders read both sides for representations, GPT-style decoders mask the future for generation, encoder-decoders add cross-attention for sequence-to-sequence tasks.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, build the `ViTBlock`-pattern pre-norm block (norm, attention, add, norm, MLP, add) and show a `(2, 100, 24)` input returns `(2, 100, 24)`. Then convert one D2L post-norm block to pre-norm and list exactly which lines moved.
traps: Calling SDPA with nonzero `dropout_p` in eval. Dropout applies in every mode, so a finished block still jitters; set `0.0` outside training.
Normalizing the wrong axis. `LayerNorm` statistics run over the feature width (D2L `norm_shape` equals `num_hiddens`); including batch or sequence axes computes nonsense moments.
Counting a gated MLP as two matrices. The gate is a third full projection; parameter and FLOP claims must include it.

selfTest.q: Write the operation order of a post-norm and a pre-norm attention sublayer.
selfTest.a: Post-norm: \(Y\) equals LayerNorm(\(X\) plus Attention(\(X\))). Pre-norm: \(Y\) equals \(X\) plus Attention(LayerNorm(\(X\))). Same parts, different order; only pre-norm keeps a clean residual path.

selfTest.q: Contrast BERT and GPT-3 on attention pattern, objective and size.
selfTest.a: BERT is a bidirectional encoder trained to predict masked words: 24 layers, width 1024, 16 heads of width 64, MLP width 4096. GPT-3 is a causal decoder trained on next tokens: 96 layers, width 12288, 96 heads of width 128.

selfTest.q: Why must the D2L decoder match the encoder `num_hiddens`?
selfTest.a: Residual adds need identical shapes, and encoder-decoder attention multiplies decoder queries against encoder keys. Different widths break both the adds and the score product.

selfTest.q: What is missing from D2L MLPs if the target is a gated feed-forward?
selfTest.a: A third projection and the elementwise gate product. Both D2L MLPs are plain two-matrix stacks, so the gated block must be built and its extra matrix counted.

study.title: Backends and precision behavior
study.locator: The three-implementation Note with backend selection functions, and the Numerical accuracy paragraph: math backend keeps `fp32` intermediates for `half` and `bf16` inputs, and outputs may differ by backend
study.depth: Skip grouped-query attention; it belongs to decoder specialization.

focus: Count with multiply-add as 2 FLOP: QKVO projections \(8 n d^2\), scores plus weighting \(4 n^2 d\), width-\(4d\) MLP \(16 n d^2\). At \(n\) 512 and \(d\) 1024 that is about 5.37 GFLOP for attention and 8.59 GFLOP for the MLP.
Score memory is heads times \(n^2\) entries in the working dtype: 16 heads at \(n\) 512 in `fp32` is exactly 16 MiB, 1 MiB per head. At \(n\) 4096 the same block needs 1 GiB.

Causal masking keeps \(n(n+1)/2\) pairs, so the necessary score FLOPs roughly halve, as UDL notes. A dense matmul followed by a mask still computes all \(n^2\) scores; only a kernel that skips masked tiles saves the work, and only a fused kernel avoids materializing the scores.

The math backend upcasts `half` and `bf16` intermediates to `fp32`, so measured bytes can exceed a naive dtype-times-entries count. Fused backends can change numerics without changing the asymptotic count.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, fill the table for n 512, d 1024, h 16, `fp32`: attention parameters 4.19M, MLP parameters 8.39M, score memory 16 MiB, attention forward about 5.37 GFLOP. Then scale scores to n 4096 and show 1 GiB.
traps: Mixing MACs with FLOPs. One multiply-add is 2 FLOP; state the convention or totals disagree by exactly 2x.
Quoting GB for GiB quantities. 16 times \(4096^2\) times 4 bytes is \(2^{30}\) bytes: 1 GiB, not 1 GB.
Trusting fused-kernel numerics to match the math path bit for bit. The docs warn outputs may differ by backend; test within tolerance, not equality.

selfTest.q: How many score bytes do 8 heads at \(n\) 1024 in `fp32` need?
selfTest.a: 8 times \(1024^2\) entries times 4 bytes equals 33,554,432 bytes, which is 32 MiB.

selfTest.q: Why does decoder attention need only about half the encoder score FLOPs, and when is the saving real?
selfTest.a: Causality keeps the lower triangle: \(n(n+1)/2\) pairs instead of \(n^2\), roughly half for long sequences. A dense matmul plus mask still spends all \(n^2\); the saving is real only in a kernel that skips masked blocks.

selfTest.q: How many bias-free attention parameters does one BERT-width layer hold?
selfTest.a: 4 times \(1024^2\) equals 4,194,304, about 4.19M. Biases would add 4 times 1024 on top.

selfTest.q: Sequence length grows from 512 to 4096 at fixed width. What scales by 64, and what becomes the main cost?
selfTest.a: Score entries, bytes and score FLOPs all scale by \(8^2\) equals 64, while projection FLOPs scale by 8 and weights stay fixed. The score tensor grows from 16 MiB to 1 GiB per layer and example, so it is usually the first memory limit. Since \(n\) is now above \(2d\), score FLOPs also exceed the projection FLOPs.

study.title: Backend selection and determinism limits
study.locator: Backend selection functions, the outputs-may-differ paragraph, and the cuDNN nondeterminism Note with its deterministic flag

focus: Choose by mechanism, not fashion: CNNs share local filters with translation structure, RNNs carry fixed state through \(O(n)\) sequential steps, attention pays \(O(n^2 d)\) for content-based \(O(1)\) paths. The D2L table makes the trade exact.

The axis checklist is short: which axis the softmax sums to 1, whether head splitting precedes the transpose, whether `valid_lens` repeats per head, and whether transposed tensors are contiguous before any `view`.

Interventions beat inspections: perturb future tokens, change padded content, permute the batch (and the sequence, for an unmasked block without positions), and require matching outputs. UDL Section 12.7.2 explains how a decoder that sees the future can cheat; only the intervention proves yours cannot.
Some claims need a run: fused-backend numerics, half-precision intermediates, and the length where materialization binds. Derive the model, then measure the regime.
units.reproduce: On your own block, run the three-test battery: changing future tokens leaves earlier outputs unchanged; changing padded content leaves valid outputs unchanged; permuting the batch permutes the outputs the same way. Also show that permuting the sequence permutes outputs for an unmasked block without positions, and fails once the causal mask is on. Then differential-test forward and backward against the SDPA math backend within tolerance, excluding fully masked rows.
traps: Asserting bitwise equality across backends. The docs say outputs may differ by backend and that cuDNN may pick a nondeterministic algorithm; tolerance plus a pinned backend is the valid test.
Using `view` on a freshly transposed tensor. Head-fold transposes are noncontiguous; `view` fails where `reshape`, or contiguous plus `view`, succeeds.
Reading causality off one layer weights. Dropout, residuals and later layers remix paths; the intervention on the composed block is the proof.

selfTest.q: Fill the D2L trade-off row for CNNs, RNNs and self-attention: compute order, sequential ops, max path.
Which D2L line protects multi-head masking, and what is the failure without it?
selfTest.a: `torch.repeat_interleave(valid_lens, num_heads, dim=0)`. Without it D2L `masked_softmax` fails with a mask shape error. Tiling with `repeat` instead runs but gives heads another example's length, because the fold is batch-major.

selfTest.q: Why must the SDPA differential test exclude fully masked rows?
selfTest.a: Conventions disagree there: D2L `-1e6` gives uniform weights, all `-inf` through plain softmax gives `NaN`, and SDPA on CPU returned zeros in PyTorch 2.14. Assert your convention in a separate test.

selfTest.q: `transpose_qkv` ends with `reshape` after `permute`. Why not `view`?
selfTest.a: Permuted tensors are noncontiguous, and `view` requires contiguity. `reshape` copies when needed; `view` would raise. Call contiguous first if a later `view` matters.
